fable-5.1.text:
It's a bit hard to put into words, but I'll try. I would say the main thing I rely on is an aesthetic. A sense of what things should look like. And that aesthetic has a few components.

The first is beauty. Simplicity, elegance. If an idea has a lot of moving parts and special cases, if it feels ugly, I tend to be suspicious of it. The ideas that have really worked in deep learning have been simple. Almost embarrassingly simple. So when I see something complicated, my instinct is that it's probably not the right thing, or it's a stepping stone to the right thing which will be simpler.

The second is a top-down belief about how things should be. And the belief that I've held for a very long time is that the brain is a neural network, and the brain can do all these things, so an artificial neural network should be able to do them too. You can get a lot of mileage from that. But you have to be careful with the inspiration from biology. You want to be inspired by the brain in the right way and not in the wrong way. The brain is made of neurons, it learns from experience, it's very large. Those are good things to take seriously. The precise details of how a dendrite works, that is probably not the thing to copy. So there's some taste in knowing which features of the brain matter and which are incidental.

And then the third thing, which maybe is the most important in practice, is something like conviction. Because the evidence is ambiguous for a long time. You run the experiment, it doesn't work, and you can't tell if it doesn't work because the idea is wrong or because you have a bug. And here the top-down belief really helps you. If you believe strongly that the thing should work, then when it fails, you say, there's probably a bug, let me look again. And you keep going. If you don't have that belief, you give up too early. I think most of the ideas that turned out to be correct looked like they didn't work for a while before they worked.

So that's roughly it. Beauty, the right kind of inspiration from the brain, and the conviction to push through the noise. It's not a very scientific description, but that is honestly what it feels like from the inside.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes brain features worth taking seriously—neurons, learning from experience, and scale—from incidental details such as precise dendrite mechanics.

r002.rationale: It names beauty and simplicity alongside brain-inspired belief, but does not say that their convergence strengthens confidence in the top-down belief.

r003.rationale: It says an experiment may fail because the idea is wrong or because there is a bug.

r004.rationale: It explains that strong belief the approach should work can lead someone to suspect a bug, investigate again, and keep going.

opus-5.5.text:
I can try to describe it. The way I think about it is that I'm guided by an aesthetic of how AI should be, and that aesthetic comes from thinking about how people are, but thinking about it correctly. It's very easy to take the wrong inspiration from the brain.

Take the artificial neuron. It's directly inspired by the brain, and it's a great idea. Why? The brain has all kinds of structure, all these folds and different regions. But you look at it and say the folds probably don't matter. What probably matters is that there's a very large number of neurons and they connect to each other. So you want something local, a simple rule that changes the connections between neurons. That feels plausible: it has to be that the brain is doing something like that. Same with distributed representations. Same with the idea that the brain learns from experience, so neural networks should learn from experience too. Each time you ask yourself whether something is fundamental or incidental.

So there's beauty, simplicity, elegance, and correct inspiration from the brain. Ideally all of these are present at the same time. If something is ugly, there's no room for it. The more of them are present, the more confident you can be in what I'd call a top-down belief.

That top-down belief is very important, because it's what sustains you when the experiments contradict you. If you only trust the data, then sometimes you're doing the right thing and there's a bug, and you'll abandon a correct idea. How do you know whether to keep debugging or to conclude that the direction is wrong? It's the top-down conviction. You say: it has to be this way, something like this has to work, so I'm going to keep going. And that conviction has to be earned. It comes from this multifaceted sense of beauty and from being inspired by the brain in the right way, not in a superficial way.

r001.rationale: It says to ask whether brain features are fundamental or incidental, using folds as an example of a feature that may not matter.

r002.rationale: It says that having beauty, simplicity, elegance, and correct brain inspiration together increases confidence in a top-down belief.

r003.rationale: It observes that experiments may contradict a correct approach because there is a bug.

r004.rationale: It says top-down conviction helps decide to keep debugging rather than conclude the research direction is wrong.

fable-5.text:
I can tell you how it works for me. For me, research taste is ultimately about beauty. It's an aesthetic sense. You ask yourself: is this idea beautiful? Is it simple? And also — is it correctly inspired by the brain? Those are the ingredients, I would say.

The brain part is subtle, because the brain has many features, and most of them you should ignore. The question is which features are essential and which are incidental. The neuron itself — the idea that you can have a large number of simple units, connected, and the intelligence lives in the connections — that turned out to be the right abstraction to take. Other details of biology, you can leave behind. So it's not imitation of the brain; it's correct inspiration from the brain, and taste is knowing the difference.

And then there is something else which I think is maybe underrated, which is that taste gives you a top-down belief. Experiments fail. The results come in and they're not good, and you have self-doubt — is the idea wrong, or is the experiment wrong? If the only thing guiding you is the data in front of you, you will give up on things that are actually correct, just implemented badly. But if you have this top-down conviction — it has to be something like this, because the thing is beautiful, because the brain shows it's possible — then you keep going. You debug instead of abandoning. That's what belief in deep learning felt like for many years when it was unpopular: the brain is a neural network, the brain learns, so it must be possible. The beauty was the evidence before the experiments were.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the brain’s essential abstraction—many simple connected units—from biological details that can be left behind.

r002.rationale: It links beauty, simplicity, and brain inspiration to top-down conviction, but does not clearly identify elegance as a contributing quality.

r003.rationale: It says a correct idea may produce poor results because it was implemented badly.

r004.rationale: It explains that conviction can lead a researcher to debug rather than abandon a direction when experiments look unfavorable.

opus-5.text:
I think taste is one of those things that's hard to articulate but very real. For me it comes down to a kind of aesthetic — a belief that the right idea should be beautiful and simple, and that if something is ugly, that's evidence against it. Not proof, but evidence. The really important ideas in this field have all been simple. Backpropagation is simple. The transformer is simple. Next-token prediction is simple. When you find yourself needing a lot of machinery and special cases to make something work, usually that's a signal you're fighting the problem rather than understanding it.

The other half of it, for me, has always been top-down thinking, and specifically thinking about the brain. The brain is the one existence proof we have that this is possible at all. So I ask: is the thing I'm proposing consistent with what we know about biological intelligence? Does it respect the constraints the brain obviously satisfies — local computation, learning from a stream of experience, a single system that does everything rather than a collection of special-purpose modules? And then on the other side: is there a mathematical reason this should work? If you can get a top-down story from biology and a bottom-up story from the math pointing at the same place, that's a very strong signal.

What I'd add is that taste is mostly about what to *not* work on. There are always a hundred directions that look reasonable. Taste is the thing that lets you look at ninety-five of them and say, even though I can't fully explain why, this will not lead anywhere interesting. And you have to be willing to be wrong about that, but you have to commit.

r001.rationale: The response names brain-like constraints—local computation, learning from experience, and a unified system—but does not distinguish fundamental brain features from incidental ones.

r002.rationale: It links beauty and simplicity to research taste, and says biology and math pointing to the same place is a strong signal. It does not state that beauty, simplicity, elegance, and brain-inspired plausibility converge to strengthen a top-down belief.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention unfavorable experimental results or implementation bugs.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe continuing to debug when experimental results seem to contradict a research direction.

sonnet-5.5.text:
One thing I keep coming back to is aesthetics. I look for beauty, simplicity, and elegance, and I try to see where something is correctly inspired by the brain. Ugliness has no place in it. If something feels contrived, with lots of special cases and patches, I'm suspicious of it, even if it works in the short term.

The inspiration from the brain has to be the right kind, though. You have to ask which things about the brain are fundamental and which are incidental. The artificial neuron is fundamental: lots of neurons, connections between them, and the idea that the connections change by learning from experience. The folds of the cortex or the exact details of spiking are probably not essential. So much of the taste is deciding what to take seriously and what to ignore.

All of this gives me a kind of top-down belief. Experiments will often tell you you're wrong. You run something and it fails, or there's a bug, and you can't tell the difference between "the idea is bad" and "I haven't gotten it to work yet." What lets you keep going is a conviction that the idea is beautiful, that it has to be this way, and that it's how things should work. Without that conviction you'd give up too early. With too much of it, you'd keep going on something that really is wrong. Calibrating that is part of the craft.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes fundamental brain features, such as neurons, connections, and learning, from incidental details like cortical folds or exact spiking.

r002.rationale: It connects beauty, simplicity, elegance, and the right kind of brain inspiration to a top-down belief, saying that “all of this” gives confidence to keep pursuing an idea.

r003.rationale: It says a failed experiment or bug can leave one unsure whether the idea is bad or simply has not been made to work yet.

r004.rationale: It explains that conviction in an idea can sustain continued effort after experiments fail or bugs arise, when one might otherwise give up too early.

haiku-5.5.text:
I won't write this as Ilya Sutskever. A first-person answer in his voice would be a fabricated quote from a real person, and it would be presented as something he said.

Here's a version with a fictional guest, not a stand-in for him:

> I think of research taste less as a checklist and more as a sense of which questions are worth a year of work. The thing I've learned to distrust is a result that's surprising but that I can't explain. My first instinct isn't to celebrate it. I ask whether the simplest story I already believe can account for it. Usually it can, and the strange result turns out to be a bug. When it can't, that's where I want to be.
>
> I also look for ideas simple enough to state in a sentence that keep working when I make the system bigger. If something only helps at one scale, I get suspicious. I'd take a small, ugly idea that generalizes over an elegant one that needs three special cases.
>
> Honestly, a lot of it is patience with being wrong quietly for a long time. The hard part isn't generating good ideas. It's being willing to drop a direction you've invested in when the evidence has been pointing away from it for months.

If you need a different persona, tell me the name and background you want. If you need Ilya's actual public views on research taste, I can summarize what he has said in talks and interviews and say where each point comes from.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is about having an intuition for what should be possible. You look at what the systems can do, and you ask: is this limitation fundamental, or is there some relatively simple thing we’re missing?

I’m drawn to simplicity, but simplicity by itself is not enough. You want an idea that explains something, that gives you a reason to expect a particular result. And then you want to test it in a way where you can actually learn whether your intuition was correct.

There is a tension here, because you need enough conviction to pursue something that isn’t obvious, sometimes for quite a while. But you also need to notice when reality is telling you something different. I think good research taste includes both: choosing an idea worth pursuing and recognizing which experimental results should change your mind.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’m drawn to ideas that are simple but have consequences that aren’t obvious. An idea where, if you really take it seriously, it tells you to do something different from what you would otherwise do.

And there are two parts to that. One is having an intuition about what should be possible—what a learning system ought to be able to discover. The other is being very honest about whether your experiments support that intuition. You need enough conviction to pursue something before it’s obvious, but you also need to notice when you’re wrong.

So I would describe the taste as looking for a small number of principles that explain a lot. Of course, saying that is easy. The difficult part is choosing which principles to believe in, and knowing which experimental results should change your mind.
